candidate_windows.window_text: In this section, we detail the implementation of our framework for graceful forgetting in generative language models, Learning With Forgetting (LWF). It consists of three components: eliciting self-knowledge, evaluating forgetting confidence, and periodically unlearning. Fig 1 illustrates the overview. For the sake of convenience in exposition, we use $\mathcal { D } _ { L }$ to represent the learning task and $\mathcal { D } _ { F }$ to denote the forgetting task. It is important to note,however, that the framework is task quantityagnostic,which will be elaborated in Section 4.

As discussed in Sections 1 and 2,although research on forgetting in broader contexts is not lacking, few existing graceful forgetting methods are specifically designed to enhance fine-tuning plasticity for pre-trained generative language models, which makes effective method migration challenging. To place LWF in a broader methodological context, we select three baseline approaches originally developed for different settings but adaptable to ours with minimal modifications: BSS(Chen et al.,2019) and SRS(Shen et al.， 2024)， two structural regularization methods that mitigate negative transfer from pretrained knowledge in nonautoregressive models; and F-learning (Ni et al., 2024),an active unlearning technique proposed for model editing in large language models. We use Llama3.2-1B (Touvron et al., 2023) as the base model. For eliciting self-knowledge, we employ a 3-shot prompt concatenated with the input question, use greedy decoding, and limit the maximum number of generated tokens to 256. For computing the forgetting confidence,we set the one-step update coefficient $\alpha = 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 }$ (as defined in Equation 4). To maintain gradient coherence during periodic unlearning,we interleave the datasets $\mathcal { D } _ { L }$ and $\mathcal { D } _ { U }$ by including one sample from $\mathcal { D } _ { U }$ for every $N _ { u }$ samples from $\mathcal { D } _ { L }$ . We set $N _ { u } = 7$ and choose $\beta$ (from Equation 5) as either O.1 or 0.05,depending on the forgetting task. The training batch size is 4,which results in one unlearning sample appearing every two batches.We optimize using AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with a learning rate of $1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }$ ,and train for one full epoch. All experiments are conducted on eight NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs with full-parameter finetuning.For further implementation details,please refer to Appendix A and our source code repository https://github.com/rubickkcibur/LWF.

Tables 6,7,8,9,and 10 present the few-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT） prompts designed for each dataset, which are used during both selfknowledge elicitation and evaluation. As shown in the prompts, answers are formatted with the phrase "The answer is” to facilitate automated answer extraction. Any model output that does not conform to this format is considered incorrect. When multiple instances of “The answer is”appear in the output, the first occurrence is taken as the final answer.
